title: Permit rules, confirmed from the code text
question: Which of the permit rules the other screens could not check does the code text settle, and what does it say?
finding: 10 rules were found and quoted. Among them: an unissued application expires after 730 days and an issued permit after 365 days without work; a permit to finish expired work is charged on the unfinished part only; paid premium review is open to anyone and refunded if late; work without a permit costs nine times the issuance fee plus the permit fee; consultants report only on jobs over $1,000,000; and the departments must review material in the order received unless a written finding says otherwise.
how: Each section was found by its heading in the full-text export, and every quotation was matched word for word against that section (the script stops if one is missing). The fee amounts were checked in the printed tables 1A-B and 1A-K.
limits: The export shows the code as last amended; two of these sections were amended by an ordinance effective 22 June 2026, so earlier years may have had other limits. A rule in the code says what must happen, not what did. Departmental guidelines (for example the written order-of-receipt exceptions) are not in the code and are not on disk.

rows.rule: An application on which no permit has been issued expires 730 days after filing; the Building Official may extend it by 180 days at a time, for a fee (Table 1A-J), on written request showing justifiable cause.
rows.quote: shall be deemed to have been abandoned, and shall expire, 730 days after the date of filing if no permit has been issued
rows.answers: permit_process toConfirm: life of an application

rows.rule: An issued permit becomes void 365 days after issue if work has not started, or after work stops for 365 days in a row; one 180-day extension for a fee, more for justifiable cause.
rows.quote: any permit shall expire and become null and void 365 days from date of issuance if the work authorized
rows.answers: permit_process toConfirm: life of a permit

rows.rule: To finish work under an expired permit a new alteration permit is needed; its fee is based on the value of the work not yet done, and no new plan review fee is charged when the original plans are followed.
rows.quote: The permit fee shall be based upon the valuation of the uncompleted work.
rows.answers: permit_process toConfirm: whether a finish-only permit is charged on the full job value
rows.verdict: Confirmed: charged on the unfinished part, not the whole job

rows.rule: A site permit must be issued before the first addendum is submitted, and each addendum must be approved and issued before its work starts; all addenda must be issued within the permit’s time limit or everything is cancelled.
rows.quote: The site permit must be issued prior to submittal of the first addendum.
rows.answers: permit_process toConfirm: which approvals must come first
rows.verdict: Confirmed for site permits and addenda

rows.rule: Paid faster review is open to any applicant who asks and pays: Building Inspection guarantees a first-review date set case by case, and refunds the extra fee on written request if it misses. Table 1A-B prints the fee as 50% of the plan review fee plus $1,000.
rows.quote: If the Department fails to complete its plan review within the guaranteed plan review time, the additional fee paid shall be refunded
rows.answers: permit_process toConfirm: what premium plan review costs and who may use it

rows.rule: Work begun without a permit triggers an investigation fee before a permit can issue. Table 1A-K prints it as nine times the permit issuance fee plus the original permit fee; it may be cut to two times the permit fee for work done before the current owner.
rows.quote: The Building Official may reduce the investigation fee to two times the amount of the permit fee
rows.answers: permit_process toConfirm: penalty for work without a permit
rows.verdict: Confirmed (the Controller’s two and nine times both appear in the code)

rows.rule: A permit consultant must register and report only for paid work on a "major project" (construction cost over $1,000,000 needing a Building Inspection or Planning permit) or on an Entertainment Commission permit. Architects and engineers of record and the contractor are excluded.
rows.quote: any project located in the City and County which has actual or estimated construction costs exceeding $1,000,000
rows.answers: permit_process toConfirm: whether consultants must report all work or only large projects
rows.verdict: Confirmed: only major projects and Entertainment Commission permits; small-job consulting is not reportable

rows.rule: Building Inspection, Planning and Public Works must treat all applicants the same whether or not they hire a permit consultant; intentional preference is official misconduct.
rows.quote: Intentional preferential treatment of any permit applicant and/or the applicant’s representatives by any officer or employee
rows.answers: fastlane, permit_metrics: the standard a fast lane is measured against

rows.rule: The three departments must process applications, revisions and corrections in the order received unless there is a written public-policy finding (public money in the project, a City error, disability-access work); each department must keep written guidelines.
rows.quote: in the order in which that type of material is received unless there is a written finding of a public policy basis
rows.answers: permit_process toConfirm: how reviews are assigned and ordered
rows.verdict: Confirmed: order of receipt, with written exceptions

rows.rule: A street-space permit for construction cannot run longer than the building permit allows for the work; an extension of the building permit does not bind Public Works.
rows.quote: in no event may the duration of the proposed occupancy under the street space occupancy permit or any extensions thereof be longer
rows.answers: permit_process toConfirm: whether street permits and building permits each require the other (catch-22)
rows.verdict: Partly: the street permit depends on the building permit’s time limit; no sentence here makes the building permit wait for the street permit

sources.t: American Legal Publishing: San Francisco Charter and Municipal Codes, full-text export (saved 17 Nov 2026)
